drills.q: Your Dockerfile does COPY . /app then RUN pip install -r /app/requirements.txt. What's wrong and how do you fix it?
drills.a: Any source file change invalidates the pip install layer's cache because COPY . /app's content hash changes, forcing a full reinstall every build. Fix: COPY requirements.txt first, RUN pip install, then COPY the rest of the source.

drills.q: A teammate baked an API key into an image via ENV, then removed it in a later RUN with `rm`. Is the image safe to push now?
drills.a: No. Layers are immutable and additive; the rm only adds a whiteout in a later layer masking the file in the merged view, the earlier layer containing the key is still fully present and extractable via docker history or layer inspection. Rebuild without the secret ever touching a layer (BuildKit --mount=type=secret) and rotate the leaked key.

drills.q: CI build takes 18 minutes on ephemeral runners with no persisted disk between jobs. --mount=type=cache is already in the Dockerfile but doesn't seem to help. Why, and what's the fix?
drills.a: Local BuildKit cache mounts persist on the builder host's disk; ephemeral runners get a fresh disk every job, so there's nothing warm to hit. Fix: use a remote cache backend, e.g. --cache-to type=registry,ref=... / --cache-from, or GitHub Actions' type=gha backend.

drills.q: Why can't you `FROM scratch` a dynamically linked Go binary that wasn't built with CGO_ENABLED=0?
drills.a: scratch has no libc, no loader, nothing — a dynamically linked binary needs the shared libraries and dynamic loader present at runtime, which scratch doesn't provide. Either build statically (CGO_ENABLED=0) or use distroless/base which includes glibc.

drills.q: Security review flags 340 CVEs, several critical, in your production image built FROM ubuntu:22.04. What's your triage order?
drills.a: Generate/inspect the SBOM to see exact package+version per finding and whether each is OS-level (inherited from base) or an app dependency. Check reachability — is the flagged code path actually invoked. Patch genuine risks; document scoped, time-boxed exceptions for confirmed-unreachable findings. In practice, switching to a multi-stage + distroless final image resolves the large majority immediately since most findings live in OS packages the app never touches.

drills.q: What's the practical difference between a build-time scan passing and an admission-controller policy also requiring image signatures?
drills.a: Build-time scanning only guarantees the image was checked at that moment in that pipeline. Admission-time signature verification (Kyverno/Gatekeeper rejecting unsigned images) is the last gate that catches an image pushed via a different path entirely, or a build-time scan that was skipped or bypassed upstream — provenance, not vulnerability content.

drills.q: Fifty microservices all build FROM python:3.13-slim. Does standardizing the base image actually save anything at the cluster level given each image is a separate artifact?
drills.a: Yes — layers are content-addressed and shared per-node: the shared base layer is stored and pulled once per node regardless of how many images reference it, so new deploys/scale-ups on a node with a warm cache only pull each image's unique layers. Standardizing bases compounds this; picking fifty different bases loses the sharing entirely.

drills.q: A distroless-based container works fine locally (built with the :debug tag) but the team wants to exec into the production (non-debug) image to check a stuck process. What should they do instead?
drills.a: Use an ephemeral debug container: kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=busybox --target=<container-name>, which shares the target container's process namespace without modifying the running production image or reintroducing a shell into it permanently.

drills.q: Explain why xz-utils (CVE-2024-3094) is the reference incident for supply-chain tooling like SBOMs and image signing, and what each would and wouldn't have caught.
drills.a: A trusted-seeming maintainer identity inserted an obfuscated backdoor into build scripts of a widely-depended-on compression library, activating specifically in distro release builds. An SBOM would show the dependency/version present but not that the build process itself was compromised. Provenance/signing (SLSA-style attestation of exactly how and from what source an artifact was built) is what would make 'was this built the way the public source claims' independently verifiable — the two are complementary, not substitutes.
